```{r libraries, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```



#Problem 2

```{r read_in_packages and tidy data, message = FALSE}
accel = read_csv("./data_hw3/nhanes_accel.csv",
                  na = c("", ".", "NA"),
                 col_types =cols(
                   SEQN = col_factor()
                 )) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()


covar = read_csv("./data_hw3/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4,
  na = c("", ".", "NA"), 
  col_types = cols(
    sex = col_factor(),
    education = col_factor(),
    SEQN = col_factor(),
    age = col_integer()
    )) |> 
    drop_na( BMI, age, education, sex) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()


covar_accel = right_join(accel, covar,  by = "seqn") |> 
  filter(age>=21)

```


```{r female_male_education}
gender = covar_accel |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      "1" ~ "Male",
      "2" ~ "Female"
    )) |> 
  mutate(
    education = case_match(
      education,
      "1" ~ "Less_than_Highschool",
      "2" ~ "Highschool",
      "3" ~ "More_than_Highschool"
    )) |> 
  mutate(
    education = forcats::fct_relevel(education, c("Less_than_Highschool", "Highschool", "More_than_Highschool"))
    ) |>
  mutate(
    sex = as.factor(sex)
  ) |> 
  arrange(education) 

gender_edu_t = gender|> 
  distinct(seqn, sex, education, age) |> 
  janitor::tabyl(education, sex) 

gender_age_edu_p = gender |> 
  distinct(seqn, sex, education, age) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "white", color = "royalblue4") +
  facet_grid(sex~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distributions for Men and Women per Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Number of participants"
  )
theme_set(theme_minimal())

gender_edu_t
gender_age_edu_p
```
Before creating a table of gender vs education level, I first created a gender data frame that would be used for all problem 2 related graphs and tables. For this dataframe, I ensured legibility by renaming the numerical factors of sex and education to their corresponding literal labels. I then ensured that the education level followed a linear progression from less than a highschool education to more than a highschool education. This gender table shows the counts of each participant by gender and education level. The majority of the participant are in the highest education level possibly leading to skewed end results. Except for higschool level, with a slight skew towards men, there is almost no difference in the gender of the participant in each education level.

To create the gender vs education table, I piped in the gender dataframe. I then ensured that no seqn value was double counted by passing it into the distinct function. Finally the resulting data was piped into the tabyl function to create a reader friendly table of counts of education level by sex. The resulting table lists counts of participants by gender and education level.

To create a histogram of the number of age distributions for men and women in each education category, I first piped in the gender data frame and ensured unique counts of the participant by their seqn id. I then created a histogram of the resultant data. I specified that it must be a histogram. Faceting by sex and education, I created a side by side comparison of these distributions. For aesthetics I converted the theme to be more minimal, widened the bins, filled the inside white and colored the outsides blue. The resulting diagram shows 6 separate histograms showing the counts of participants by age. There are 2 rows, delimited by gender, and 3 columns delimited by education level. The color scheme matches the school spirit. This histogram reaffirms that there are higher counts of the highest education level in this study. In lower education sections there are sparser age categories. There seems to be more of a balance between gender.


```{r activity_level by age_sex/education}

act_level_p = gender |> 
   group_by(seqn) |> 
  mutate(
    total_activity = sum(mims)
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  distinct(seqn, total_activity, age, sex, education) |> 
   ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex))+
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Activity Level by Age, Comparisons of Sex and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "24-Hour Activity"
  )
  
act_level_p
```
To create a plot comparing total activity level by age, with a further comparison by sex and education, I piped in the previously created gender data frame. From this I aggregated the mims across the minutes of the day to create a total activity level variable. To ensure that no seqn values were double counted, I passed the resulting table through the distinct function. I then created a scatterplot of the total activity vs age of the participant. This plot was faceted by education and a comparison of gender was done by coloring by this variable. I finally added a title, and renamed the x/y axes. This plot shows the relation between total activity and the age of the participant. An additional comparison is made across sex and education level. A clear decrease of total activity can be seen with the increasing age. This decrease is steepest within lower education levels, with a more gradual decrease for more educate participants. While sex is closer together in the least educated, the gender dichotomy is more apparent as the education level progresses. Females were found to have higher activity levels compared to their male counterparts in these higher education levels.

```{r activity_level over the day}
act_over_day = gender |> 
  select(minute, mims, sex, education) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(gsub("min", "", minute)),
  ) |> 
  group_by(sex, minute, education) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth()+
  facet_grid(~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Activity Level Over the Day, Comparison of Sex and Education",
    x = "Minutes",
    y = "MIMS"
  )
act_over_day
```
From this resultant graph I can see an indication that participants who have less education have slightly higher mims over the daytime period (the 500-1250 minute time interval), but no strong conclusions can be made. In the less than high school education participants, there is less of a dichotomy over gender with male and female lines mainly overlapping. In more educated segments the gender dichotomy is more apparent with females having observably higher mims over the same daytime period. When transitioning into the night (the 1250-250 minute time interval), activity declines substantially.

##Problem 3


```{r citi_bike_load_in}
citi_01_20 = read.csv("./data_hw3/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate( month = "january",
          year = "2020")

citi_07_20 = read.csv("./data_hw3/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()|> 
  mutate( month = "july",
          year = "2020")

citi_01_24 = read.csv("./data_hw3/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()|> 
  mutate(month = "january",
          year = "2024")

citi_07_24 = read.csv("./data_hw3/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()|> 
  mutate( month = "july",
          year = "2024")

citi_total = bind_rows(
  citi_01_20,
  citi_01_24,
  citi_07_20,
  citi_07_24,
) |> 
  mutate(
    ride_id = as.factor(ride_id),
    rideable_type = as.factor(rideable_type),
    year = as.factor(year),
    weekdays = as.factor(weekdays),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual),
      month = factor(month)) |> 
  drop_na(duration,
          start_station_name,
          end_station_name)
  
head(citi_total)

```
When combining all tables, the resultant data frame is a `r nrow(citi_total)` by `r ncol(citi_total)` table. There are nine variables in total. They describe the month, year, weekday, starting and stopping station of the ride. The data also describes the ride type, membership of the rider, and rider's id. The following variables are factors: year, month, weekday, member_casual, rideable_type. Only duration is a numerical variable. The following are character variables: start_station_name, end_station_name


```{r rides_per_year_month_member_casual}
rides_per = citi_total |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  summarize(
    rides = n()) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = rides
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
rides_per
```
This table shows the number of rides that each type of member did in July/January of 2020 and 2024. The number of rides has had a over a 10 fold increase in casual riders from January 2020 to July 2024. During this same time period member's rides have trippled. From January to July 2020, the number of causal bikers halved while member bikers had slight gains. While in January 2020 members had a 10 fold lead over casual members, by July 2024 they only maintain a 3 fold lead.

```{r most_popular_stations}
pop_stats = citi_total |> 
  filter(
    year == "2024",
    month == "july"
         ) |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(
    rides = n()) |> 
  arrange(
    desc(rides)) |> 
  head(5) |> 
      knitr::kable(digits = 3) 

  
pop_stats
```


```{r ride_duration by timeframe}

weekday_durn = citi_total |> 
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(
    median_durn = median(duration)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = str_c(
      c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
      ))) |> 
      arrange(weekdays) |> 
  ggplot(aes( x = weekdays,median_durn, color = month
  )) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_grid(~year)+
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))+
  labs(
    title = "Median Duration over Weekday, Month, Year",
    x = "Weekday",
    y = "Median Duration (mins)")

  weekday_durn
```
From this graph we can see that 2020 had a higher median ride duration compared to 2024. Similarly there is a higher median ride duration in July when compared to January for both these years, however the difference is more stark in 2024. While Saturday and Sunday seemed to have the longest median duration compared to all other weekdays for both years, the only exception was for Sundays in January where they dropped below all other medians.



```{r duration by month, membership status, bike type}

durn_2024_p = citi_total |> 
  filter(year == "2024") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x= member_casual,y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(
    title = "Duration by Membership, Bike-Type, and Month ",
    x = "Membership Type",
    y = "Duration (mins)") +
      coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,150))
durn_2024_p
```
Casual riders seem to have a longer ride duration compared to member riders. While close in value, there seems to be slightly longer ride duration in July than January. While classic bikes generally have a longer ride duration, during the month of July there seemed to be a slight increase of electric bike ride duration over classic bikes. All groups seem to expeirence a high amount of longer duration outliers, indicating a strong skew.
